date.label: Undated thematic Leviticus legislation
date.note: This is a literary and thematic grouping in the Sinai narrative, not an independent datable event. No absolute year is inferred.

claims.claim: The received text presents five main offering complexes and priestly handling rules.
claims.evidence: Lev 1:1–7:38; biblical description, not independent confirmation of historical practice.

claims.claim: Leviticus 1 prescribes herd, flock, and bird options for burnt offerings.
Leviticus 2 permits several preparations of grain offerings and specifies salt, oil, and frankincense in their respective contexts.
The well-being offerings include sacrificial fat portions and shared meal contexts.
The label ḥaṭṭāʾt is translated sin offering in many traditions and purification offering in influential modern scholarship.
claims.evidence: Leviticus 4–5 (KJV, full chapters); Gane 2022 full encyclopaedia discussion and Janzen 2008 full article text in Religion Compass 2(1), pp. 38–52 consulted; translations/sacrificial-function theories are debated.

claims.claim: The reparation offering regulations include specified restitution in cases involving sacred property and certain wrongs against neighbors.
Placing the offering instructions before priestly ordination serves a didactic literary purpose.
claims.evidence: Narrative sequence Lev 1–10; Gane 2022; inferred editorial function.

claims.claim: No single scholarly theory provides an uncontested explanation of every Israelite sacrificial action; Janzen explicitly reports a lack of consensus in the field.
claims.evidence: Janzen 2008 full scholarly article text consulted, Religion Compass 2(1), pp. 38–52, together with Gane 2022 inspected encyclopaedia sections; schools of sacrificial explanation are varied; absence of universal consensus must not be turned into absence of meaning.

connections.note: Ordination instructions anticipate the offering rites used in Leviticus 8.
The rites become operative in the priestly inauguration narrative.
Sacrificial rules continue with accompanying grain and drink offerings.
Calendar sacrifices adapt multiple offering types to recurring occasions.
Comparison shows both common sacrificial concerns and significant differences over slaughter.
The prophet condemns worship detached from justice, not necessarily sacrifice in itself.
The psalm juxtaposes a broken spirit and acceptable sacrifices; interpretive connection.
Hebrews presents a later Christian Christological reading of sacrificial language; not an independent report of Leviticus-era practice.
